definitions.plain_definition: A mathematical proof that says any system of math that is powerful enough to do basic arithmetic cannot prove that it is free of contradictions using only its own rules.
definitions.used_in_context: Gödel's Second Incompleteness Theorem guarantees that no sufficiently powerful formal system can prove its own consistency using its own axioms.

definitions.plain_definition: A set of rules and symbols used to do math or logic, like a game with strict rules.
definitions.used_in_context: The universe — which IS a formal system running on mathematical laws — cannot prove its own ground from within itself.

definitions.plain_definition: Basic starting assumptions in math or logic that are accepted as true without proof.
definitions.used_in_context: no sufficiently powerful formal system can prove its own consistency using its own axioms.

definitions.plain_definition: A number in physics that describes the energy density of empty space, which affects how fast the universe expands.
definitions.used_in_context: The cosmological constant is tuned to 1 part in 10¹²⁰.

definitions.plain_definition: A number that describes how strongly particles interact with light, and it is crucial for atoms to exist.
definitions.used_in_context: The fine structure constant to 1 part in 10⁴⁰.

definitions.plain_definition: The idea that certain numbers in physics are set exactly right for life to exist, and even tiny changes would make the universe uninhabitable.
definitions.used_in_context: The precision that makes 'coincidence' mathematically absurd.

definitions.plain_definition: Kurt Gödel, a mathematician who proved that in any sufficiently powerful math system, there are true statements that cannot be proven within that system.
definitions.used_in_context: Five independent proofs — Gödel, Tarski, Turing, Second Law, Landauer — demonstrate that no system can prove its own consistency.

definitions.plain_definition: Alfred Tarski, a logician who proved that no language can define its own truth without leading to contradictions.
definitions.used_in_context: Five independent proofs — Gödel, Tarski, Turing, Second Law, Landauer — demonstrate that no system can prove its own consistency.

definitions.plain_definition: Alan Turing, a computer scientist who proved that there is no general method to determine whether a computer program will ever stop running.
definitions.used_in_context: Five independent proofs — Gödel, Tarski, Turing, Second Law, Landauer — demonstrate that no system can prove its own consistency.

definitions.plain_definition: Rolf Landauer, a physicist who showed that erasing information always produces heat, meaning information processing has a physical cost.
definitions.used_in_context: Five independent proofs — Gödel, Tarski, Turing, Second Law, Landauer — demonstrate that no system can prove its own consistency.

definitions.plain_definition: The Second Law of Thermodynamics, which says that in a closed system, disorder (entropy) always increases over time.
definitions.used_in_context: Five independent proofs — Gödel, Tarski, Turing, Second Law, Landauer — demonstrate that no system can prove its own consistency.

definitions.plain_definition: A measure of disorder or randomness in a system; the Second Law says entropy always increases in a closed system.
definitions.used_in_context: The Second Law of Thermodynamics, which says that in a closed system, disorder (entropy) always increases over time.

definitions.plain_definition: A system that does not exchange energy or matter with anything outside itself.
definitions.used_in_context: Closed systems cannot sustain themselves.

definitions.plain_definition: The quality of being logical, consistent, and holding together in a unified way.
definitions.used_in_context: The universe maintains order, truth, consistency, and coherence despite five theorems proving it can't do this alone.

definitions.plain_definition: The property of a system where no contradictions can be derived from its rules.
definitions.used_in_context: no system can prove its own consistency.

definitions.plain_definition: An endless chain of causes where each cause requires a previous cause, never reaching a starting point.
definitions.used_in_context: self-existent (or we have infinite regress).

definitions.plain_definition: Something that must exist and cannot not exist; its non-existence is impossible.
definitions.used_in_context: The external ground must be: necessary (or the system collapses).

definitions.plain_definition: Something that exists by its own nature and does not depend on anything else for its existence.
definitions.used_in_context: self-existent (or we have infinite regress).

definitions.plain_definition: Existing outside of time, without beginning or end.
definitions.used_in_context: eternal (it precedes the universe).

definitions.plain_definition: The fundamental reality that underlies and supports everything that exists.
definitions.used_in_context: the ground of all being, the source of truth and order and beauty and goodness.

definitions.plain_definition: The traditional qualities that describe God in Judeo-Christian theology, such as being all-powerful, all-knowing, and perfectly good.
definitions.used_in_context: These are precisely the classical attributes of God as described in Judeo-Christian theology for thousands of years.

definitions.plain_definition: The study of God based on the shared religious traditions of Judaism and Christianity.
definitions.used_in_context: These are precisely the classical attributes of God as described in Judeo-Christian theology for thousands of years.

definitions.plain_definition: Trust or confidence in something that is not based on complete proof, but on evidence and relationship.
definitions.used_in_context: That last step has a name too. It's called faith.

definitions.plain_definition: A logical or mathematical demonstration that shows something must be true.
definitions.used_in_context: the same math proves it can't prove Him.

definitions.plain_definition: A statement that has been proven to be true using logic and mathematics.
definitions.used_in_context: That would make God a theorem, not the ground of being.

definitions.plain_definition: A system of parts working together like a machine, often implying something that operates without consciousness or purpose.
definitions.used_in_context: That's not God. That's a really impressive mechanism.

definitions.plain_definition: The process of performing mathematical calculations or logical operations, often by a computer.
definitions.used_in_context: relationship could be replaced by computation.

definitions.plain_definition: The fundamental structure or design that underlies the universe.
definitions.used_in_context: the entire architecture of reality — is that it runs on relationship, not mechanism.
